title: Drink, Drugs, Phones & Distraction
whatItIs: Alcohol, drugs and hand-held devices all reduce a driver's control. The law sets limits and bans, and the phone ban also covers anyone supervising a learner.

keyFacts.text: You MUST NOT drive with alcohol above the legal limit. The limits in Scotland are lower.
You MUST NOT drive under the influence of drugs or medicine, or above set drug limits.
You MUST NOT use a hand-held phone when driving or supervising a learner, even when stopped in traffic.
You MUST keep proper control at all times, including with sat nav or driver assistance systems.

keyFacts: Hand-held device offence: 6 points and a £200 fine. New drivers lose their licence.

a.label: Illegal: hand-held use
points: Calls, texts, photos, browsing, even offline or in flight mode
Also at traffic lights or queuing in traffic

b.label: Allowed
points: Hands-free (headset, voice, mount) if never held
Hand-held to call 999 or 112 when unsafe to stop, or when safely parked

onTheTest.question: Your pupil is waiting at a red light. You read a text on your hand-held phone. Which is correct?
options: Illegal: the ban covers supervising a learner, even when stopped
Legal, because the car is stationary
Legal, if the phone is in flight mode
Only the pupil, as the driver, can be prosecuted
onTheTest.why: Rule 149: you must not use a hand-held phone when driving or supervising a learner. The law applies when stopped at lights or offline.

onTheTest.question: An examiner has good reason to think a candidate is under the influence of drink. What does DT1 say to do?
options: Call the police and end the test
Carry on and record a dangerous fault
Say they appear ill and the test can't go ahead, not mentioning drink
Ask the candidate to take a breath test
onTheTest.why: DT1 6.49: the examiner says the candidate appears to be ill and the test cannot go ahead, avoiding any reference to drink or drugs.

traps: Below the limit is not safe: alcohol reduces driving ability even under the legal limit.
You may still be unfit to drive the morning after drinking the previous evening.
Hands-free is legal but still distracting; it is far safer not to use any phone while driving.
A prescribed medicine over its limit: there is a medical defence only if driving was not impaired.

jurisdictionNotes.text: Lower drink-drive limits: 22 microgrammes per 100 ml of breath, 50 mg per 100 ml of blood.
